name: Laundromat business
blurb: Run a self-service laundry with washers and dryers, plus optional wash-and-fold service
title: Laundromat Business: How to Start, Costs and Risks
description: How to start a laundromat: how it makes money, what equipment, lease and utility checks you need, who it suits, the main risks and how to test a site first.
answer: A laundromat rents time on commercial washers and dryers to people who do not have their own, and often adds wash-and-fold, dry cleaning drop-off or vending. It is capital-heavy: equipment, plumbing and a long lease are the big commitments, and water, power and rent costs decide whether the machines ever pay for themselves.

body: Customers pay per wash and per dryer cycle, by coin, card or app. Extra income comes from wash-and-fold priced by weight or bag, pickup and delivery, and vending for detergent and snacks.

Out of that come rent, water, sewer, gas or electricity, repairs, insurance, cleaning and any staff. Utilities and rent are the costs that most often catch new owners out, so get real bills before you commit.

ul: A site with suitable zoning, enough water supply, drainage, power and venting for commercial machines. Ask the landlord and the local utility, not just the agent.
Commercial washers and dryers, new or used, plus payment systems, folding tables and seating.
A lease you can live with: length, rent increases, who pays for plumbing changes and what happens if you need to leave.
Local permits and checks: rules differ. Examples include a business licence, building and plumbing permits for the fit-out, and wastewater rules in some areas.
Insurance for equipment, property and public liability, and a plan for cleaning and repairs.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Investors with savings who can carry slow early months
People without capital or credit for equipment
Owners comfortable with leases, contractors and repairs
People who want a local service with steady routine
Anyone unwilling to read utility bills and lease clauses

ul: Rent and lease terms: a long lease with rising rent can outlast your equipment's profit.
Utility costs can rise and vary by site; old plumbing or venting can be expensive to fix.
Buying an existing laundromat: ask for real utility bills, machine age and takings records, not the seller's summary. Do proper due diligence.
Franchise and equipment-package pitches: read the full contract and fees. In the US, the FTC says a franchisor must give you its disclosure document at least 14 days before you sign or pay.
Competition from nearby laundromats and from in-building laundry rooms.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Map existing laundromats near your target area and visit them at peak times.
Count how many nearby homes are apartments without in-unit machines.
Ask a landlord and the local utility what it would take to supply water, drainage and power to a candidate site.
Get quotes for equipment and fit-out, and ask for real utility rates.
Offer a small wash-and-fold service from an existing laundromat to see if people will pay.
Have a lawyer or adviser read the lease before signing.
Line up permits, contractors and equipment delivery dates.
Set up payment, cameras and a cleaning and repair routine.
Price washes after checking competitors and your utility costs.
Track takings per machine and utility use each week from day one.

faq.a: No. Machines break, the store needs cleaning, customers need help and utilities need watching. Owners can hire staff, but that cuts the margin.

faq.q: Should I buy an existing laundromat or build a new one?
faq.a: Buying gives you a track record, but only if you verify it with real utility bills, machine records and bank statements. Building lets you choose the site and equipment but takes longer to fill.

faq.q: What makes a good laundromat location?
faq.a: Dense housing where many homes lack their own machines, easy parking or walking access, and a lease and utility setup you have checked yourself.
